justification: The passage states that wear 'gathers in the length that sweeps the ground and in the two or three links either side of the swivel', which is exactly the two locations B names. A is contradicted by 'a chain condemned for losing a fifth of its diameter is usually condemned on a single bad metre' - the loss is local, not uniform across every link. C (salt corrosion) is never mentioned, and D transfers 'the inshore aids, where the water is narrow' from Cadell's concession about scope onto wear, which the text never says.

Scope buys a circle: 'wind and tide swing the buoy about its sinker, and the more chain it has, the wider the ground it can wander over, so the light is somewhere inside that circle rather than on the cross printed on the chart.' A displaced buoy is therefore normally riding inside its allowed circle rather than having dragged its sinker, which is C. B reverses the stated relation (more chain, not less, widens the wander), A turns the single 31 m / 11 m example into a rule, and D is not addressed.

The lightship paragraph exists to show that positional uncertainty long predates the loggers: her logs carry three bearings watch after watch 'because a moored ship does not sit still either and her keepers knew it', and Fewtrell says 'We knew the shoal was under us... Where we were over it was another question.' That is A. B is the opposite of what the text says, C invents a post-war account of manned stations disappearing, and D draws a comparison with today's crews that the text never makes.

The text says plainly: 'Cadell has read the recordings and concedes the inshore aids, where the water is narrow. On the outer stations he has not moved.' That is D. A overstates the concession into abandonment, B invents a cost argument where his stated reason is that a short-moored buoy 'takes the sea in its chain rather than in the water, and it is the chain that fails', and C invents a chronology the text does not give.

The article follows a tender lifting and relaying buoy 43, explains why a mooring must be slack and what that slack costs in positional accuracy, then sets Cadell against Prigent and closes with 'Neither record disposes of the other.' That is B. A and D take single details (the lightship; crew costs) for the whole, and C makes the piece an argument for loggers, which its even-handed close refuses to be.

A founder 'bills bronze by the kilo and tuning by the hour', and the text gives both ends: 'On a thirty-kilo bell the tuning can come to more than half of what the parish pays; on a bell of a tonne, where the same five partials take not much longer to find, the bronze is the larger part of the bill.' That is exactly D. A ('always') is killed by the tonne case, B by the two separate billing bases, and C by 'take not much longer to find'.

Corvenden 'tunes the hum, the prime and the nominal closely and leaves the minor third near where the casting put it' - three partials tuned close, the minor third left as cast, which is B. A describes Voregg, who brings all of them 'inside four cents of the figures the theory gives'; C is not in the text; D inverts which partial she leaves alone.

Because thinning only lowers a partial and 'Nothing pulls it back up', 'That one-way arrow is why founders cast heavy' - the bell leaves the mould with 'an allowance of metal... that exists only to be turned away'. Tuning all five tightly therefore requires that metal to be there first, which is A. B is contradicted by 'Each partial answers to a band of metal at a particular height inside the bell', C is not addressed, and D's 'always' overstates a claim the text presents as contested.

The writer sets out Voregg's tolerances and Corvenden's objection, reports the one trial that bears on it - 'There is some evidence for her, and Voregg does not pretend there is not' - then gives Voregg's caveat and notes that the decisive experiment 'costs two bells, and no parish has ordered it'. He picks no side, which is C. B fails because the text names an experiment that would settle the question; A overreads a trial the writer explicitly qualifies; D is the reverse of the text.

The piece explains the five partials and how thinning tunes them, prices that work against the bronze, and then shows that 'How far to chase those five is where the trade divides' - that is D. A takes the cost paragraph for the whole and misstates it for heavy bells, B inflates a subordinate remark about tin loss into the subject, and C is not addressed.

The school's row is 'a row of boxes in the same position on the same kind of gable' that 'fills most summers', which is C. A hardens 'most summers' into every summer, B invents fitting dates for both rows that the text never gives, and D is not addressed.

Talbourne's loggers show the animals 'high and deep in the warm hours, when the young grow fastest, out towards the cooler eaves at night', which is D. A reverses that pattern, C is contradicted by 'by dawn the whole void has given its heat back', and B's heat rising from the rooms below is never mentioned.

'Both of those two sat on a chimney breast whose flue still carried warm air up from the block's boiler, and the loggers inside them recorded a swing much like the timber's' - the range came from the flue behind, not from the box, which is A. B is contradicted by 'cast boxes on two other south-facing walls, with nothing behind them but insulation, stayed empty', and those same empty boxes also sink C. D is not in the text.

The writer grants the timing objection exactly as far as the early record goes - 'On the early boxes she was plainly right, and Talbourne says so' - and then reports the second series, which held timing constant ('all fitted out of season') and still split timber from cast. That is C. A is contradicted by that second series, D by the writer's explicit agreement with her, and B invents a complaint about the size of her file search.

The piece opens on eleven years of empty boxes at the laundry against a row that 'fills most summers' four streets away, and spends the rest weighing thermal range against fitting season as the explanation - that is B. A and D mistake the planning and council framing for the subject, and C misreads three summers of logging temperatures as giving up counting altogether.

The text states it directly: 'Den som fick en tunna råg i mars skulle vid skörden lämna tillbaka lika mycket, jämte ett tillägg — vanligen en åttondel — också det i råg.' That is C. A is contradicted by 'Ingen sedel behövde växlas', D by 'Vad magasinet däremot inte kunde göra var att sprida risken', and B invents an annual assessment where the text gives a customary eighth.

'Den som inte hade betalat tillbaka till Mikaeli, i slutet av september, fick stå över utlåningen följande vår' supports A word for word. B is contradicted by the two locks with 'skilda nycklar' held by kyrkvärden and föreståndaren and by the rule that two people be present; C by 'Varje utlåning skulle skrivas in samma dag'; D by 'den föreståndare som sockenstämman valt'.

The reviewer's objection is that the book's own appendix undercuts the savings-bank explanation: 'ligger de tidigaste nedläggningarna i Hässle härad flera decennier före den första sparbanken i samma härad'. That is D. A is false because he does mention kommunreformen 1863, C is contradicted by 'nedläggningen i tre av de socknar han följer sammanfaller väl med sparbankens tillkomst', and B misattributes the single-document method, which belongs to the Bjärnhult episode about practice rather than to the argument about decline.

She raises the reused buildings to make a point Grimlund only notes in passing: 'Att en socken kunde göra sig av med inrättningen men behålla huset säger något om vad man ansåg vara värt att spara, och jag hade gärna läst tjugo sidor till om just det.' That is B, complaint included ('som om det vore en avvikelse från ämnet. Det är det inte'). A is contradicted by that same passage, C reverses the fault she finds, and D is not in the text.
